notes.meaning: Being invited to eat with a ruler or powerful leader is an honor, but it requires great caution. A guest must pay close attention to what is happening and stay aware of who is hosting the meal. The luxury of the table can easily distract someone from the dangers of the royal court.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often note that this warning closely resembles Chapter 23 of an ancient Egyptian text called the Instruction of Amenemope, though they debate whether one text borrowed from the other or if the likeness is coincidental.

notes.meaning: Solomon warns the guest to control his appetite with absolute seriousness. Putting a knife to one's throat is an everyday picture for holding back strong desires with strict self-restraint. Losing control of your cravings in front of a ruler shows weakness and can lead to trouble.

A wise person does not lose control over the rich, expensive dishes offered by a ruler. Such food is called deceptive because the host may have hidden political motives or be testing the guest. What looks like pure generosity might really be an invitation designed to discover your weaknesses.

Solomon urges his hearers not to wear themselves out just to pile up money. Working hard to provide for daily needs is good, but making riches your main goal destroys inner peace. True wisdom means knowing when to stop and being content with what God provides.

Worldly riches are temporary and can disappear in a moment. Solomon compares wealth to a great eagle that quickly sprouts wings and flies out of sight into the sky. Setting your heart on money brings disappointment because earthly goods cannot give lasting security.

The writer warns against accepting a meal from a selfish, grudging person. In biblical times, this kind of person was said to have an evil eye, meaning he is stingy and wants everything for himself. Even if his food looks delicious, enjoying his hospitality will only bring trouble.

A stingy host may politely invite you to eat, but inside he is counting the cost of every mouthful. His warm words do not match his real feelings because he resents every bite you take. A person should look at a host's true character rather than trusting sweet words.

Once you realize how begrudging the host is, the food will make your stomach turn. You will wish you had never accepted his invitation at all. All the polite thanks and kind conversation you offered him will feel completely wasted.

Solomon advises against trying to teach someone who stubbornly refuses to learn. A hardened fool will only mock good advice and look down on sound instruction. Sharing precious truths with such a person is like throwing pearls before pigs, as Jesus later taught.

Property boundaries in ancient Israel were marked with stone markers, and moving them secretly stole land from neighbors. This command specifically protects orphans who have no earthly father to defend their fields. Taking advantage of the weak and defenseless is a serious sin in God's eyes.

Although orphans seem defenseless, the almighty God acts as their near kinsman and defender. A redeemer was a family protector responsible for rescuing relatives and regaining lost property. The Lord is strong enough to plead their case in court and bring justice against anyone who harms them.

Learning wisdom requires active effort and personal attention. A person must not merely sit and listen with their physical ears, but must gladly welcome truth into their heart. True understanding grows when someone is eager to be taught and ready to obey.

Parents are urged to correct their children promptly when they do wrong rather than holding back out of false pity. Proper, loving correction does not harm a child, but instead keeps them safe from dangerous habits. Guiding a young person with firmness helps them grow into a healthy, sensible adult.

Faithfully correcting a child helps rescue them from destruction. In the Bible, Sheol refers to the place of the dead, showing that undisciplined rebellion can lead to an early grave or spiritual ruin. Wise guidance given during childhood can steer a young person away from paths that end in eternal judgment.

A godly parent or teacher feels deep happiness when a child chooses the way of wisdom. True wisdom begins inside the heart and transforms the way a person thinks and lives. Nothing brings greater comfort to a loving father than seeing his child walk in truth.

The teacher expresses deep personal joy when his student speaks truth and good sense. The ancient phrase for the inmost being pictures a person's deepest emotions and soul. When wisdom fills the heart, it naturally shows itself in honest, upright speech.

God's people must never feel jealous of the temporary wealth or freedom that wicked people seem to enjoy. Instead, believers should live all day long in the fear of the Lord, which means having reverent awe, love, and trust toward God. Keeping your focus on God keeps your heart from desiring sinful lifestyles.

Those who trust the Lord have a guaranteed future and an everlasting reward. The prosperity of the wicked soon ends, but the believer's hope of peace and life with God will never be destroyed. Knowing that God keeps His promises gives lasting courage through present hardships.

Solomon calls his child to pay close attention to instruction and actively lead his heart on God's path. Wisdom is not passive; it requires deliberate choices to keep one's thoughts and desires on what is good. When the heart is directed properly, daily actions and steps follow the right way.

The teacher warns against keeping company with heavy drinkers and people who gorge themselves on rich food. Associating with those who lack self-control makes it easy to pick up their destructive habits. A wise person practices temperance and avoids wild, unrestrained gatherings.

Wasting money on excessive food and drink quickly empties a person's pockets and leads to poverty. Overeating and drinking also produce laziness and constant sleepiness, leaving a person unfit for honest work. In the end, a life of careless indulgence leaves a person wearing rags and in complete need.

Children should respect and listen to their parents, remembering with gratitude the gift of life and care they received. Even when an aging mother grows frail, her wisdom and years of experience should never be dismissed. Honoring elderly parents is a lifelong duty blessed by God.

Solomon urges his hearers to gain truth, wisdom, and understanding no matter what effort or cost it requires. Once you have acquired God's truth, you must never trade it away for money, ease, or worldly popularity. Divine truth is the most valuable treasure a person can possess.

A parent experiences immense gladness when their child grows up to live an honest and godly life. Worldly achievements can bring temporary pride, but genuine righteousness brings lasting joy to a family. Raising a child who chooses wisdom is one of the greatest blessings a father can receive.

The proverb turns into an earnest wish for the student to live in a way that blesses his parents. Living wisely and doing what is right brings comfort and peace to a mother and father in their later years. A good life is the greatest honor a child can give to those who raised them.

Wisdom, speaking through the teacher and reflecting God's own voice, asks for total trust and love. God does not just want outward religious rituals; He desires our whole heart and deepest affection. When our hearts are given completely to Him, we take genuine delight in following His ways.

Solomon pictures an immoral woman as a deep pit or a narrow well from which escape is almost impossible. Giving in to sexual sin traps a person in guilt, shame, and destruction. What may look appealing on the outside leads into a suffocating trap that ruins lives.

A seductive woman lies in wait like a bandit waiting to ambush unsuspecting travelers. She robs men of their integrity, their family honor, and their devotion to God. Her influence causes many people to break their marriage vows and abandon their faithfulness.

Solomon asks six sharp questions to picture the misery, grief, arguments, and injuries that plague certain people. The questions describe broken bodies, senseless fights, and bloodshot, dull eyes. This vivid description prepares the listener to see the destructive outcome of a specific foolish habit.

The answer to the questions points directly to people who spend long hours drinking alcohol and looking for strong, spiced drinks. Sitting around drinks dulls a person's senses and drags them into the painful troubles described just before. Alcohol promises pleasure but delivers sorrow to anyone who gives themselves over to it.

The writer warns against staring longingly at rich, sparkling wine as it swirls attractively in the cup. Looking at it with greedy desire fuels temptation and weakens a person's self-control. True wisdom means stopping sin at its very beginning before it takes hold of your will.

Even though fine wine seems smooth and pleasant at first, its ultimate outcome is deadly. Solomon compares excessive drinking to the venomous bite of a snake that secretly spreads poison through the whole body. The temporary pleasure of intoxication ends in sharp physical and spiritual pain.

Drunkenness confuses a person's sight and scrambles their ability to think clearly. It leads to strange delusions, fuels lustful desires, and loosens the tongue to speak crude and foolish words. When alcohol takes over the mind, shame and self-control disappear.

A drunk person acts as completely heedless of danger as someone trying to sleep on rolling ocean waves or high up on a ship's rocking mast. Such a sailor is in constant peril of falling overboard and drowning without even realizing it. Intoxication makes people feel completely secure even while standing on the brink of disaster.

The drunkard wakes up bruised and battered from fights he cannot even remember, yet he remains numb to his own misery. Even after suffering terrible harm, his only desire is to shake off his stupor and search for another drink. This pictures the terrible grip of addiction, where a person stubbornly returns to the very thing destroying him.
